{{Short description|Example of a phase-space star product in mathematics}}
{{About-distinguish-text|the product on functions on phase space|the [[star product]] on graded posets}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Moyal product''' (after [[José Enrique Moyal]]; also called the '''star product''' or '''Weyl–Groenewold product''', after [[Hermann Weyl]] and [[Hilbrand J. Groenewold]]) is an example of a '''phase-space star product'''.  It is an associative, non-commutative product, {{small|★}}, on the functions on <math>\mathbb{R}^{2n}</math>, equipped with its [[Poisson bracket]] (with a generalization to [[symplectic manifold]]s, described below).  It is a special case of the {{small|★}}-product of the "algebra of symbols" of a [[universal enveloping algebra]].

==Historical comments==
The Moyal product is named after [[José Enrique Moyal]], but is also sometimes called the [[Hermann Weyl|Weyl]]–Groenewold product as it was introduced by [[Hilbrand J. Groenewold|H. J. Groenewold]] in his 1946 doctoral dissertation, in a trenchant appreciation<ref>{{cite journal |last= Groenewold |first= H. J. |date= 1946 |title= On the Principles of elementary quantum mechanics |url= http://www.rug.nl/research/vsi/events/groenewold/groenewold-article.pdf |journal= Physica |volume= 12 |pages= 405–460}}</ref> of the [[Wigner–Weyl transform|Weyl correspondence]].  Moyal actually appears not to know about the product in his celebrated article<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Moyal | first1=J. E.
| date=1949
| title=Quantum mechanics as a statistical theory
| journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]]
| volume=45
| issue=1
| pages=99–124
| doi=10.1017/S0305004100000487 | bibcode=1949PCPS...45...99M}}</ref> and was crucially lacking it in his legendary correspondence with Dirac, as illustrated in his biography.<ref>{{cite book |last= Moyal |first= Ann |date= 2006 |title= Maverick Mathematician: The Life and Science of J. E. Moyal |url= http://epress.anu.edu.au/maverick_citation.html |publisher= ANU E-press}}</ref> The popular naming after Moyal appears to have emerged only in the 1970s, in homage to his flat [[phase-space formulation|phase-space quantization]] picture.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Curtright |first1= T. L. |last2= Zachos |first2=C. K. |date=2012 |title= Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space |journal= [[Asia Pacific Physics Newsletter]] |volume= 1 |pages= 37 |arxiv= 1104.5269 |doi= 10.1142/S2251158X12000069}}</ref>

==Definition==
The product for [[smooth function]]s {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}} on <math>\mathbb{R}^{2n}</math> takes the form
<math display="block">f \star g = fg + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \hbar^n C_n(f,g),</math>
where each {{mvar|C<sub>n</sub>}} is a certain bi[[differential operator]] of order {{mvar|n}}, characterized by the following properties (see below for an explicit formula):
* <math>f \star g = fg + \mathcal O(\hbar),</math> Deformation of the pointwise product — implicit in the formula above.
* <math>f \star g - g \star f = i\hbar\{f,g\} + \mathcal O(\hbar^3) \equiv i\hbar \{\{f,g\}\},</math> Deformation of the Poisson bracket, called [[Moyal bracket]].
* <math>f \star 1 = 1 \star f = f,</math> The 1 of the undeformed algebra is also the identity in the new algebra.
* <math>\overline{f \star g} = \overline{g} \star \overline{f},</math> The [[complex conjugate]] is an [[antilinear]] [[antiautomorphism]].
Note that, if one wishes to take functions valued in the [[real numbers]], then an alternative version eliminates the {{mvar|i}} in the second condition and eliminates the fourth condition.

If one restricts to polynomial functions, the above algebra is isomorphic to the [[Weyl algebra]] {{mvar|A<sub>n</sub>}}, and the two offer alternative realizations of the [[Wigner–Weyl transform|Weyl map]] of the space of polynomials in {{mvar|n}} variables (or the [[symmetric algebra]] of a vector space of dimension {{math|2''n''}}).

To provide an explicit formula, consider a constant [[Poisson bivector]]  {{math|Π}} on <math>\mathbb{R}^{2n}</math>:
<math display="block">\Pi = \sum_{i,j} \Pi^{ij} \partial_i \wedge \partial_j,</math>
where {{math|Π<sup>''ij''</sup>}} is a real number for each {{mvar|''i'', ''j''}}. 
The star product of two functions  {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}} can then be defined as the [[pseudo-differential operator]] acting on both of them,
<math display="block">f \star g = fg + \frac{i\hbar}{2} \sum_{i,j} \Pi^{ij} (\partial_i f) (\partial_j g)
 - \frac{\hbar^2}{8} \sum_{i,j,k,m} \Pi^{ij} \Pi^{km} (\partial_i \partial_k f) (\partial_j \partial_m g) + \ldots,</math>
where {{mvar|ħ}} is the [[reduced Planck constant]], treated as a formal parameter here. 

This is a special case of what is known as the [[universal enveloping algebra|Berezin formula]]<ref>{{cite journal |last= Berezin |first= Felix A. |date= 1967 |title= Some remarks about the associated envelope of a Lie algebra |journal= Functional Analysis and its Applications |volume= 1 |page= 91 |author-link= Felix Berezin}}</ref> on the algebra of symbols and can be given a closed form<ref>{{cite web |last= Bekaert |first= Xavier |date= June 2005 |title= Universal enveloping algebras and some applications in physics |url= http://www.ulb.ac.be/sciences/ptm/pmif/Rencontres/ModaveI/Xavier.pdf |type= Lecture notes |publisher= Université Libre du Bruxelles, Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques}}</ref> (which follows from the [[Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula]]). The closed form can be obtained by using the [[Matrix exponential|exponential]]:
<math display="block">f \star g = m \circ e^{\frac{i\hbar}{2} \Pi}(f \otimes g),</math>
where {{mvar|m}} is the multiplication map, {{math|1=''m''(''a'' ⊗ ''b'') = ''ab''}}, and the exponential is treated as a power series,
<math display="block">e^A = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{n!} A^n.</math>

That is, the formula for {{mvar|C<sub>n</sub>}} is
<math display="block">C_n = \frac{i^n}{2^n n!} m \circ \Pi^n.</math>

As indicated, often one eliminates all occurrences of {{mvar|i}} above, and the formulas then restrict naturally to real numbers.

Note that if the functions {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}} are polynomials, the above infinite sums become finite (reducing to the ordinary Weyl-algebra case).

The relationship of the Moyal product to the generalized {{small|★}}-product used in the definition of the "algebra of symbols" of a [[universal enveloping algebra]] follows from the fact that the [[Weyl algebra]] is the universal enveloping algebra of the [[Heisenberg algebra]] (modulo that the center equals the unit).

==On manifolds==
On any symplectic manifold, one can, at least locally, choose coordinates so as to make the symplectic structure ''constant'', by [[Darboux's theorem]]; and, using the associated Poisson bivector, one may consider the above formula.  For it to work globally,
as a function on the whole manifold (and not just a local formula), one must equip the symplectic manifold with a torsion-free symplectic [[Connection (mathematics)|connection]]. This makes it a [[Fedosov manifold]].

More general results for ''arbitrary Poisson manifolds'' (where the Darboux theorem does not apply) are given by the [[Kontsevich quantization formula]].

==Examples==
A simple explicit example of the construction and utility of the {{small|★}}-product (for the simplest case of a two-dimensional euclidean [[phase space]]) is given in the article on the [[Wigner–Weyl transform]]: two Gaussians compose with this {{small|★}}-product according to a hyperbolic tangent law:<ref>{{cite book |editor-last1= Zachos |editor-first1= Cosmas |editor-last2= Fairlie |editor-first2= David |editor-last3= Curtright |editor-first3= Thomas |date= 2005 |title= Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space: An Overview with Selected Papers |publisher= World Scientific |location= Singapore |series= World Scientific Series in 20th Century Physics |volume= 34 |isbn= 978-981-238-384-6 |editor-link1= Cosmas Zachos |editor-link2= David Fairlie |editor-link3= Thomas Curtright }}</ref>
<math display="block">
\exp\left[-a\left(q^2 + p^2\right)\right] \star \exp\left[-b\left(q^2 + p^2\right)\right] =
 \frac{1}{1 + \hbar^2 ab} \exp\left[-\frac{a + b}{1 + \hbar^2 ab} \left(q^2 + p^2\right)\right].
</math>Equivalently,<math display="block">e^{-\tanh (a) \frac{q^2 + p^2}{\hbar }} \star e^{-\tanh (b) \frac{q^2 + p^2}{\hbar }}
= 
\frac{\tanh (a + b)}{\tanh (a) + \tanh (b)} e^{-\tanh (a+b) \frac{q^2 + p^2}{\hbar }}</math>The [[classical limit]] at <math>\hbar \to 0, a/\hbar \to \alpha, b / \hbar \to \beta</math> is <math>e^{-\alpha(q^2+p^2)} e^{-\beta(q^2+p^2)} = e^{-(\alpha + \beta)(q^2+p^2)}</math>, as expected.

''Every correspondence prescription'' between phase space and Hilbert space, however, induces {{em|its own}} [[Transformation between distributions in time–frequency analysis|proper]] {{small|★}}-product.<ref>{{cite book |last= Cohen |first= L |date= 1995 |title= Time-Frequency Analysis |publisher= Prentice-Hall |location= New York |isbn= 978-0135945322}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last= Lee |first= H. W. |date= 1995 |title= Theory and application of the quantum phase-space distribution functions |journal= Physics Reports |volume= 259 |issue= 3 |pages= 147 |doi= 10.1016/0370-1573(95)00007-4 |bibcode= 1995PhR...259..147L}}</ref>

Similar results are seen in the [[Segal–Bargmann space]] and in the [[theta representation]] of the [[Heisenberg group]], where the creation and annihilation operators {{math|1=''a''<sup>∗</sup> = ''z''}} and {{math|1=''a'' = ''∂''/''∂z''}} are understood to act on the [[complex plane]] (respectively, the [[upper half-plane]] for the Heisenberg group), so that the position and momenta operators are given by <math>
 q =\frac{a + a^*}{2} 
</math> and <math>
 p =  \frac{a - a^*}{2i}
</math>.  This situation is clearly different from the case where the positions are taken to be real-valued, but does offer insights into the overall algebraic structure of the Heisenberg algebra and its envelope, the Weyl algebra.

==Inside phase-space integrals==
Inside a phase-space integral, just {{em|one}} star product of the Moyal type may be dropped,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Curtright |first1=T. L. |last2= Fairlie |first2= D. B. |last3= Zachos |first3= C. K. |date= 2014 |title= A Concise Treatise on Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space |publisher= [[World Scientific]] |isbn= 9789814520430}}</ref> resulting in plain multiplication,  as evident by [[integration by parts]], 
<math display="block">\int dx\,dp\;f\star g= \int dx\,dp ~f ~g,</math>
making the cyclicity of the phase-space trace manifest. This is a unique property of the above specific Moyal product, and does not hold for other correspondence rules' star products, such as Husimi's, etc.
